utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start, I have a question for the Defence. I don't know whether you're going to deal with it, Mr. Stojanovic. Could you give us an indication, if we continue tomorrow with Witness RM322, how much time would you need or could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we requested six hours. I think we are on the third or fourth hour, and I hope that I will be able to complete in two or two and a half hours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two, two and a half hours, that would leave sufficient time for a re-examination if needed. That is understood. Thank you. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The next witness the Prosecution will call is Momir Nikolic. And may I take this opportunity to introduce Julian Nicholls to the Chamber. It's his first time appearing on this case. And there are no protective measures for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Welcome, Mr. Nicholls. Then I do -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Sorry to interrupt. I just wanted to say also that Virginia Lindsay, counsel for Momir Nikolic, is with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome, Ms. Lindsay. I take it that your task will be to take care that Rule 90(E) is properly applied. That is that if there is any risk for self-incrimination, that you'll deal with those matters and not to coach in any way the witness when testifying. That's -- I see that you're nodding yes so apparently we agree on the matter. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, before the examination will start, I'd like to inform you about Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And I'll read it to you, and if you have any questions remaining, don't hesitate to ask. Rule 90(E) reads, a witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony. It means that you can object to answer a question if a truthful answer might incriminate yourself, especially in order not to expose yourself to further prosecutions but the Chamber may insist on you answering that question. Mr. Nicholls, if you're ready you may proceed. You'll first be examined by Mr. Nicholls, you'll find Mr. Nicholls to your right. Mr. Nicholls is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I want to do first, very briefly, is go through a little bit of your background for the Trial Chamber. You were born in Bratunac in 1955; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you briefly tell us, just briefly, about your educational background and what your occupation was before the war started in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, before we invite the witness to answer that question, I assumed that this is Mr. Nikolic but I think that's the first question, apart from where and when he was born, who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am Momir Nikolic. I was born on 20 February in 1955, in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly asks that Mr. Nikolic repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to talk about my professional background? That was your first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think the interpreters just missed that you were born in Bratunac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Bratunac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then, yes, if you could please just briefly tell us your educational background and your occupation before the war started in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I completed my elementary and high school in Bratunac where I was born. After completing high school, I went to serve my military term of duty. When I -- at the time, usually you would serve the military term of duty after completing high school. I served in Postojna in Slovenia. After 15 months I returned to Bratunac, and then after that, I enrolled at the Faculty of Political Sciences, University of Sarajevo, which I completed in the Department of Defence and Protection. After four years I returned to Bratunac and my first job was in the high school centre Djuro Pucar Stari where I worked as a professor of defence and protection. The next five years I worked at the high school centre, and then sometime in 1986, I transferred to the Territorial Defence staff, where I worked until the war broke out, i.e. until 1992, when I was officially mobilised into the military unit where I proceeded to serve as an officer. I left the army with the rank of sergeant, and I was a platoon commander. After completing my university and transferring to the territorial staff HQ, I was promoted to officer where I was the assistant commander of the TO HQ for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, without going into the specific reasons, is it right that from roughly the end of May to November 1992, you were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In late 1992 -- actually in May 1992, I was in Belgrade, and then I returned to Bratunac in November, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in November 1992, when you returned, is it right that you became assistant commander for intelligence and security in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. After a certain period of time, pursuant to the proposal by my brigade commander, I was appointed to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was your post in July 1995, as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the time I was appointed until demobilisation, I was at the position of the chief of the organ for intelligence and security in the 1st Light Infantry Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your rank in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, I held the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And currently, you are serving a prison sentence of 20 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Moving on now to May 2003, it's correct that you pled guilty in this court to count 5 of your indictment, crimes against humanity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993 [as interpreted] I pleaded guilty to count 5 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just very briefly, during your discussions with the Office of the Prosecutor, at the time of your plea, did you at one point falsely claim personal involvement in some offences, in some crimes, which you were not involved in? Can you briefly explain that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Attached to my document or documents that I signed with the Prosecution, there is a statement. The contents of that statement are correct. Because of the Trial Chamber, I would just like to clarify briefly what this is about. The first thing that is in the statement is the identification of a photograph, my own photograph, and I did not have any intention, absolutely no intention, of placing myself where that soldier was or anything like that. So it was truly a person who absolutely looks like me, was in uniform in that place. At that time, at the very beginning, when we began the interviews my attorneys showed me that photograph and I said yes, the picture does resemble me, but the circumstances were not clear to me as to where this was exactly. When I found out that this was in the region of Sandici, I said that I never was there outside of my vehicle. I was there in the critical period but I was never there outside of my vehicle. And then we -- simply when we talked or when I talked with the Prosecution I simply did not want to rule out the possibility that I was there. I did not simply want to, as I say, a priori, say I was not there. Simply I said, yes, it's possible that it's me in that picture, and it was clear to me then that it was not me when my lawyers investigated the matter, went out to the area, and found the person who really is in that photograph and that is Mile Savic, aka Cuko, from the Special MUP Brigade. And then we presented that documentation, myself and my lawyer, to the Prosecution, we said that is that person and it is not really me. But in view of the fact that I said that I was there, I accepted and agreed to sign the statement and I accepted that at the time when we talked I really did say what I did say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, would you please slow down so that the interpreters have time to translate all your words? Otherwise we will miss part of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 19004, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you take a look at that document, Mr. Nikolic, is that declaration the document that you signed that you were just discussing?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the statement that I signed as part of all the documentation that I signed with the Prosecution. May I continue with the following thing that I would like to explain that I would wish to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. Very briefly. Same thing. When the negotiations with the Prosecution were in their final stages, the Prosecution -- actually I and the Prosecution were going through various documents, countless times, different events, and of course the Prosecution insisted on the truth. I come from an organ which precisely knows how investigations are conducted. I'm familiar with the problems. And that is why I understand the attempts of the Prosecution to get to the truth that they were interested in. At one point in time, actually several times, we talked about Sandici and about Kravica and the events there. Each time I said that I had nothing to do with the crime in Kravica, and at one point we got to that topic again and I was upset, I was angry, and because I didn't know what else to say, anything else, revolted, I said yes, I was there. And then at one point I understood what I did. We interrupted the interviews, there was a day of break, and I told my lawyers that I would like to apologise to the Prosecution and tell them that that was a mistake. And then after a day we met again, I gave my apologies, and after that we continued to talk and everything that I said I did say. I said everything that I knew, so I believe that that is the truth as I saw it. So on that matter, therefore, the Prosecution said that I still would need to sign so that what I said would be still on the record, documented. I said that was all right, I have no problem with that, that I made the mistake, and that I need to accept responsibility for that, and I signed that. And that is the entire truth, as far as this matter is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19004 receives number P1503, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have 65 ter 19002, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nikolic, do you need help with your headphones? I'm not sure if they are comfortable for you the way they are.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's all right, it's all right, it's all right. Here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what's coming up is your plea agreement that you made, the written plea agreement, with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could just go to the last page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And simply do you see your signature on the document, sir? I'll wait for the Serbian version to come up.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is this the plea agreement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have page 4 of the English, page 5 of the Serbian, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as part of your plea agreement, did you agree to testify truthfully in trials when called upon to do so by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you focus on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could show Mr. Nikolic paragraph 11, we need to go to the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It states: "It is understood and agreed by Momir Nikolic and the Prosecution that all information and testimony provided by Mr. Nikolic must be absolutely truthful. This means that Momir Nikolic must neither minimise his own actions nor fabricate someone else's involvement." And my question is, do you stand by that provision of the agreement and do you understand that's your obligation today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I stand by it and I know exactly what my duty is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19002 receives number P1504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence, no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Without going through it, since your plea, you've testified in quite a few trials?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm now moving on to a new topic and speaking about the period around July 1995, the summer of 1995. I'd like to have you explain to the Trial Chamber what your duties were in your capacity in the security and intelligence organ of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. So first of all, just to clarify, in the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, you were chief of security and intelligence. Was that usual or in other brigades of the VRS were those duties sometimes divided between two people? Sorry, that was kind of a long question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, I was in the 1st Light Bratunac Infantry Brigade as the chief of the organ for intelligence and security. It's true that in brigades such as infantry brigades, those two functions were separate, and are carried out by two officers. In my brigade -- or, rather, in light infantry brigades, from what I know these two functions were merged and carried out by one officer. As for the remit of our work, as the intelligence security officer in the light infantry brigade, I carried out the following duties: Intelligence work. I carried out tasks in counter-intelligence. Then I worked in command staff security, those matters. Then I was also dealing with military police duties as well as criminal, legal matters. So briefly speaking, all these are responsibilities of the intelligence security organ in the light infantry brigade. If we look at it in percentages, the intelligence security organ in the light infantry brigade in practice, percentage-wise carries out tasks and assignments approximately -- intelligence and counter-intelligence jobs account for some 80 per cent and all the other things I mentioned, the staff administrative, police and criminal duties account for some 15 to 20 per cent of the total work. If you're interested in details of these activities, I can talk about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's good for now. Thank you. Was there a person named Zlatan Celanovic in the brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very briefly, what was his role and if any way did it intersect with your duties in the intelligence and security organ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief as possible. Mr. Celanovic, as per war assignment, was part of the organ for religious and moral affairs. However, in practical terms, he was engaged with -- in the military police. Why? Because in the light infantry brigade, security and intelligence organs do not act as authorised officials. We did not have official IDs as opposed to similar personnel in infantry brigades. The area of law and criminal procedure, that is to say, drafting criminal reports and gathering documents as well as preparing criminal reports to be submitted to the commander for signature, all that was done by Zlatan Celanovic while I was in the Bratunac Brigade . In addition to that, Zlatan Celanovic interrogated 98 per cent of the cases, I believe. He interrogated all those who were taken prisoner or fled from the Muslim-held territory to our territory. So he interrogated prisoners and gathered documents and information on potential war crimes carried out by Muslim soldiers who were captured, or committed by some persons who fled over to the side -- the Bratunac Brigade side. After he would complete all of these tasks, he submitted criminal reports to the brigade commander for signature. The reports on interrogations and the case files pertaining to other offences pertaining to members of the Bratunac Brigade were forwarded to the brigade commander and myself. That was the scope of his activity. When all of that was done, certain reports that were signed were handed over by him to the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, briefly, I'm going to ask you some questions about reporting -- your reporting duties and the way the command structure worked. Who was your direct commander in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My commander in July 1995 was my brigade commander, Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you would report to him then?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Whenever there was a need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about the so-called professional or expertise chain of reporting? In other words, the intelligence and security organs. Was there any reporting you did up to the Drina Corps level, to the intel and security chiefs there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did submit reports. If I may, I'd like to explain it in two sentences because I believe it requires some attention. Security organs are commanded by the officer in whose unit you were. In my case it was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. He commanded me, he issued commands to me, as the chief of the organ. Professional management is a different concept, and in that regard, we are managed by our first superior in the superior command, the person in charge of security and intelligence. In my case, it was the sector for intelligence and security in the command of the Drina Corps. When it comes to reporting, usually during daily briefings, I reported to my commander about all matters and information pertaining to my scope of authority, that is to say, security and intelligence. Depending on the needs, daily reports were drafted, sent to the professional body that manages my organ, that is to say, the sector for security and intelligence of the Drina Corps. That was standard procedure. However, there were exceptions. If information is crucial, that is more general in scope, then only the area of responsibility of one's brigade or corps, and if you believe the Main Staff should be appraised of it, then you send a report. If it has to do with security, then you send it to the security department of the Main Staff, either to the chief or the sector itself, and then that piece of information is automatically sent to the Drina Corps command, to the sector for intelligence and security, as well as the sector for intelligence and security of the Main Staff. That is the professional line of reporting when it comes to security and intelligence organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just quickly, who was your superior in the professional line, in the security branch in the Drina Corps? Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I sent my reports to the sector of the Drina Corps. Two officers worked there. One of them was Vujadin Popovic and the other, Mr. Kosoric. They were the two officers in the sector within the Drina Corps in the period you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that Svetozar Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Popovic and Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very quickly, which of these two men was in the security organ and which was in intel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From what I know, and I still believe it to be true, Popovic was in the security organ and Mr. Kosoric was in charge of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to move on a bit now, just a few questions about the military police in the Bratunac Brigade. Was there a military police platoon in the brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The military police commander in Bratunac was Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just quickly, who was his superior? Who would issue him commands?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the military police, there too are two things that need to be clearly distinguished. First of all is who is in command of the military police and who professionally manages the military police. The military police is directly commanded by the officer in whose unit the military police unit is. In my case, direct command of the military police was in the hands of Vidoje Blagojevic. In professional terms, the military police is directly managed by the security organ. The security organ in my brigade was me. My task was to propose the use of the military police to the commander, to keep an eye on combat readiness of the military police, and to keep an eye on the implementation of tasks or task issued by the commander. These are the basic three tasks in all respects when it comes to professional management over the military police in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. But just to be clear, then, the final person who has a say over what tasks the military police should carry out, is it you or the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I said that the commander had command over the military police, this entails precisely that. The commander is the person issuing orders to the military police through the military police commander in the MP platoon in the case of my brigade. So the commander is the one who issues tasks and orders the use of the military police and everything else when it comes to the concept of command over the military police. The security chief does not have a possibility to command the military police or to issue orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to another topic now, still focusing on your duties during 1995, and we'll get to July soon, did you act as a liaison officer to DutchBat and to various humanitarian organisations in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. On top of the duties I had, which is the head of the security and intelligence organ, I also carried out tasks entrusted or actually ordered to me by the brigade commander, when a check-point was set up at the Yellow Bridge, the duties of liaison officer. My task was to be in contact with members or representatives of DutchBat, that is to say, of the UNPROFOR peacekeeping forces in the protected area of Srebrenica. Also, as the liaison officer, I was in contact with all those who had an office in the enclave, in Srebrenica. This includes the military observers, the international civilian police, the Medecins Sans Frontieres, the ICRC, and I think there was a representative who was in charge of humanitarian assistance and was also a UNHCR representative in Srebrenica. During that time, as of the moment when the Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone, I was the liaison officer who was in contact with the aforementioned organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And I'll break this up now and ask you some questions first about your duties in regard to DutchBat and later with the other organisations, but, first of all, you mentioned the Yellow Bridge check-point. Could you briefly tell the Trial Chamber the location of that Yellow Bridge, the check-point you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can even show you where it is on the map, but to put it in the simplest terms, it is on the border between the check-point of DutchBat and the territory that was controlled by my, that is to say, the Bratunac Brigade. The distance between the two check-points was about between 100 and 150 metres. Geographically speaking, it was five to six kilometres from Bratunac. From Potocari -- no, I would say four kilometres away from Bratunac and perhaps three kilometres away from Potocari. I'm not sure whether I got the kilometres precisely. But the important thing was that the Yellow Bridge was along the demarcation line between the forces of the VRS, where our positions are, and UNPROFOR forces protecting the enclave. It was precisely in the area where my 2nd Infantry Battalion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could just briefly, as briefly as you can, give us a short overview of what the topics were of your conversations and contacts with DutchBat? When you met with DutchBat, and let's focus on 1995, what would you talk about with them? What were their issues, what were your issues?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only answer in principle because each of our meetings or actually the reason for a meeting was different every time. However, in principle, the biggest problems we discussed were those that had to do, first of all, with violations of the border of the demilitarised zone, by either side. We met and discussed things when victims were not soldiers and were unarmed. Seldom did we meet and discuss when there was an exchange of fire and when there were wounded and casualties on the demarcation line, when it came to soldiers. We also met when we, or they, had a problem with entry or exit in or from the enclave. The Serb forces occasionally violated the borders of the zone by setting up a new position, and then in such cases we would meet with the DutchBat representatives who required that the Serb forces withdraw to their original position. In other cases, Muslims in groups made incursions deep inside Serb territory, setting up ambushes, carrying out sabotage actions, when, as a result, civilians were often wounded who moved along roads in vehicles, but soldiers as well. We also met when it came to their requests, if there were some issues to be raised regarding rotations of their companies. So, for example, they had a plan to rotate one of their companies on a specific date and did not receive permission. In that case, they would send their request to me and I would forward it to the Main Staff and the corps command to deal with the issue or at least to provide an answer to their request. When it comes to other organisations, representatives of the ICRC, the physicians without frontiers, the UNHCR, et cetera, I was always in contact with all of them, and there were different issues at different times. Let me cite one issue per organisation. For example, the ICRC --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question, I think, was about subjects of discussion with DutchBat. Now, the witness apparently -- unless this is exactly what you wanted to ask from him, but I noticed that short and focused questions might lead to shorter answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're quite correct, thank you, Your Honour. In fact, he, Mr. Nikolic answered the question I had about the DutchBat. My next question would have been to similarly give an overview of the types of issues that were dealt with with the humanitarian and other organisations and I will try to tailor the questions to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do it in such a way, if you ask for an overview or a brief description of something, the result usually is that we have a very long description. So focused questions might be a better use of your time, but of course it's your witness. I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So, sir, Mr. Nikolic, if you could just briefly in the next couple minutes, tell us just the big topics, the kind of usual topics, that you would discuss with the international organisations, if you can just tell us quickly kind of what -- what the issues were.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think I already answered with regard to the protection forces in the enclave. When it comes to the ICRC, we discussed the status of civilians, the captured persons on both sides, and on people who flew from the enclave. I was particularly interested in discussing the issue of Serb civilians who remained in the enclave, to have those who wanted to leave the enclave brought out. They would then bring them to the Yellow Bridge. Those who wanted to leave, I accommodated their request and reunited them with their families. Those who wanted to stay were allowed to stay. When it comes to the UNHCR, we discussed the entry of humanitarian convoys and the issues that they were facing inside the enclave. Then there were requests from the Serb side to assist, and they did so, to assist for the Serb population in Bratunac and the Muslim population in Srebrenica. As for the Medecins Sans Frontieres, I frequently discussed medical issues with them and usually they had a problem with medication, and there were requests by the Serb side as well as the Muslim side. The Muslims usually required more medication, bandages and everything. They needed to keep their health centre and the hospital running. Those are -- were more or less the issues that were discussed the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to talk to you about the period leading up before the fall or liberation of the enclave in July 1995, and what the goals were of the VRS at that time. First of all, though, just -- this may have already been in evidence, but what is the meaning of the word "Podrinje," what is the area encompassed when we say the "Podrinje"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The word "Podrinje," it includes a number of municipalities located along the River Drina. There is Gornje Podrinje, to put it in broad terms, those are the municipalities in the upper part of the Drina, that is to say, Foca, Gorazde, Visegrad, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, and Bijeljina. Well, Bijeljina is already part of Semberija but it follows the Drina. So these are the municipalities along the river. And that is the general area next to the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, is the schedule a break at 10?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A break at 10, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just quickly, if I could have 65 ter 05924.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a document you've seen before, Mr. Nikolic. It's a Bratunac Brigade command report for the brigade. It's dated 4 July 1994. And it's signed by the then commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Slavko Ognjenovic. Do you recall this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the first paragraph refers to the visit to the corps, the recent visit, by the commander of the VRS General Staff, and do you recall General Mladic visiting at that time, around that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that General Mladic visited the Bratunac Brigade in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we go now to page 2 of the English and also of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you look at the top of page 2 in your language, which begins "U Podrinju," and if we look at the bottom of the English it states: "We have won the war in the Podrinje but we have not beaten the Muslims ..." And if we could go to page 3 of the English now. "... but we have not beaten the Muslims completely, which is what we must do in the next period. We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde must be defeated militarily." Then it continues: "We must continue to arm, train, discipline and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task, the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Now, can you just comment on this section I've read out, in your understanding as it reflects the goals of the -- of the Bratunac Brigade at this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will try to answer based on what I could see and what you just read out. I will comment on it. But limiting it to my own position, my personal position, as regards the text. I'll start with this latest part of it. There will be no retreat concerning the enclave of Srebrenica. We must go forward, the enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible. This part, in my mind, is a military part and I see nothing in dispute here. It discusses the enemy. I think in military terms, and in linguistic terms, it means as it is spelled out. What I find worth discussing is the next part which has to do with the en masse expulsion from the enclave, the part that has to do with expelling the Muslims. These things should not be in this document, nor is it a military task. In my understanding, nothing that has to do with combat should not and ought not be directed against the retreating Muslim population. It can be directed against the armed forces and soldiers, those that you are engaging with, but not against a civilian population. If I didn't know what I know, if I didn't know what happened in 1995, then I would not even dispute part of what we read; but since I do know what happened with those who were supposed to be protected, that is also how I understand it, that is to say, that the goal was to empty the enclave unselectively, of course it had to be militarily defeated but the ultimate goal was to have the enclave devoid of Muslims so that they leave it entirely. That is what comes to mind reading this part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, I'll have a couple more questions on this document for you, Mr. Nikolic, after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will first take the break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom first. I think the usher and security together should take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. We will take the next break a bit earlier than usual, most likely at ten minutes past 11.00 and the break will be slightly longer, most likely 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now go to the last page, page 6 of the English, page 3 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the very end of this report, just above the commander's signature, it states: "Circulate this report among all brigade members and have them sign for it. Review the report in companies, et cetera." My question is: Was this report, in fact, disseminated to the members of the brigade as ordered?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just to be precise, I have a bad interpretation, it's an information, it's not a report. This is an information. The signatory is the then commander, Slavko Ognjenovic. This information was first worked through at the meeting of the Bratunac Brigade command in its extended composition, attended by the battalion commanders as well. After we were informed, the battalion commanders were given the task of working through this information in their battalions, company by company, so that all the soldiers could be informed about this information. And that's what was done. The person responsible for this assignment was the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs, Major Jevtic. Meaning, what you asked me, the information was entirely worked through the way the commander ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Now, you talked before about one of the issues that you discussed with DutchBat was violations of the enclave and you talked a little bit about civilian casualties on the Muslim side. What was the effect, if any, that you could see from your position as intelligence and security chief, that this information had on sniping attacks, other attacks on civilians in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In my previous answer, regarding what we talked about, I and the members of the Dutch battalion, we talked about violating the enclave frontiers and opening of fire from positions, and now I'm talking about the opening of fire from positions of my brigade. Since the Srebrenica area was declared a demilitarised zone, we were never ever able to establish peace and a complete cease-fire. So opening of fire, sniper action, fire from different weapons happened constantly, sometimes it was more intense, sometimes it was less frequent. After this information, well, this is more or less, I will be free to say that this was the green light and an alibi for those undisciplined with whom I personally, as a security organ, had problems before that, because this served, and I can say freely, simply, they were perhaps not able to, nor did they want to, differentiate between targets that should be fired at, and those that should be not fired at. Those that I had problems with I requested that they be brought in, I asked that they be punished. Those who opened fire. Mostly -- actually, fire was opened in the enclave at those who -- other than soldiers. I'm not talking about -- other than soldiers, other than those who were armed and were moving from their positions to their homes or were walking between trenches at their positions. Fire was opened at civilians who should not have been the targets of either sniper action or any other fire because now we are not talking about sniper action. We are talking about weaponry that you have in a battalion. You have an undisciplined soldier with a semi-automatic rifle who can fire in front of him some 200 to 300 metres ahead, and these are positions where they were. They were places where there were civilian houses, fields, yards, where people were going about their everyday business, they were working in their fields, mowing, so on and so forth. So it was a major problem. And according to my understanding and what I had as a problem was an intensified action at those who happened to be in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So that was a long answer, but just let me make sure I'm clear. This information, once it was passed down, you're saying gave the green light to opening fire on Muslim civilians who were in their fields and going about their business?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After this information was read out in the brigade units, in battalions, companies, platoons, then you can see for yourself from this text, regarding making life more difficult, creating impossible conditions, everything that says in that part, it says, and I personally -- I am personally talking from my own personal experience. I never could not explain to anyone on the line that they should not fire anymore into the enclave. Whatever I would say to them, I got the answer, "We have permission, the commander permitted us to do that, we should be opening fire, and what are you playing at?" This was literally, "What do you want now? We have permission from the commander." So then in the beginning I had problems with the commander also and I requested, I requested that this be suspended, that this be prevented, so that we could explain somehow what it was exactly that they could open fire at. And like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05924 receives number P1505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on now because of the time and I'm going to now ask you some questions on a different topic and that is about convoys entering the enclave and how that process worked, and we are going to talk about two sorts, humanitarian aid and supply to DutchBat. All right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 05517, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, I'll read, this is a Drina Corps command very urgent order of 24 July 1994. So 20 days after the document we just looked at. I'll try to go through this a bit quickly, sir. Now we see here on the front page, the preamble is that this order is pursuant to a briefing on 1 July 1994 to the VRS Main Staff commander by Drina Corps commander and regiment brigade commanders about the level of combat readiness in units. Regarding measures, actions and tasks relating to Muslim enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're reading, Mr. Nicholls, you should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is signed by then commander of the Drina Corps, Milenko Zivanovic. If I could go to page 2 of the English, still page 1 of the Serbian. Now, if we look at point 3: "No equipment is to be allowed into the 'enclaves' apart from food and medication which are approved by the VRS Main Staff." Below that, we see, now in Serbian page 2, I believe: "All authorised cargo and people (authorisation from the VRS Main Staff) is to be thoroughly checked at the following check-points." And then below, point B is about leaving the enclaves. Now, first of all, can you tell us if that's correct, what we see here, that the equipment allowed into the enclaves is strictly to be limited to that approved by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, we can see that can be concluded on the basis of the order, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And in practice, based on your position, being there at the time, were the orders of the Main Staff followed, as it's ordered here, in terms of what materials would be allowed to enter the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As for the check-point in Zuti Most, the whole time I and all those working at the check-point acted in accordance with the orders and the approvals we received from the Main Staff or from the coordinating body of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will talk about that more in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05517 receives number P1506, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1506 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, you started talking about it. If you can, really as briefly as you can, describe the process about how you would determine what materials would be allowed into the enclave at the check-point at the Zuti Most or Yellow Bridge? In other words, how these orders regarding what was to be admitted reached you from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm obliged to say for the sake of precision that I received orders at the Bratunac 1st Light Infantry Brigade signed by Mr. Dragan Kekic. That is one type of approval or permission. The next type was signed for the most part percentage-wise by Mr. Manojlo Milovanovic, the chief of the Main Staff. And then from time to time, I would receive orders signed by Vice-President Koljevic, by name. All those orders, regardless of who signed them, when they came to my brigade, they were to be executed and we acted strictly pursuant to the orders that we received. I don't know the ratio, I don't know the relationship in the coordinating body, in the term -- in terms of who was in charge of what, as for convoys that had to do with humanitarian aid and civilians and those that had to do with DutchBat. But I know that each order, regardless of the signature, was valid when received at our check-point. Once we received an order, it would list precisely who would be allowed to pass. There would be the first and last name, ID information of those persons, and there would be a list of the cargo per truck, the types of cargo in the truck, the quantities, the type. So regardless of whether that applied to the DutchBat or anyone else, this is how it worked. Before the convoy actually arrived to the check-point at Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me stop you there because we will look at a couple documents to illustrate what you're describing. When you said "coordinating body," you're referring there to the coordinating body in Pale, the civilian body?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the coordinating body of the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether there was a member of the Main Staff on that coordinating body?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The -- what I know is that the member of the coordinating body was Dragan Kekic. Biljana Plavsic was in that body and Dr. Koljevic. What I know from the Main Staff, and I'm not sure, is -- I think that a member of that coordinating body was Mr. Manojlo Milovanovic, the Chief of Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on now, if I could show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 05526.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document which has Main Staff, Army of VRS, on the top left, 2nd of April, 1995. It's signed by General Milovanovic, who you just spoke about, if we were to look at the -- you can see that on your page -- no, not on your page but we'll get to that. And it states -- well, first I'd like you to read the handwritten part on the top right. Tell us what that says.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: "Not a single convoy or ICRC team or MSF may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence." And then the signature is Momir Nikolic, which is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. What it says here, that's what I wrote, and it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is to the command of the Drina Corps, SRK and IBK, and it says at the top: "We hereby inform you that we consent to the request of the RS coordinating body for HP emergency services as follows." And now if we look at the bottom, item number 3, I won't read it out for time's sake, but if you take a look at that it talks about how many pencils, how many markers, how many staples. Is that the kind of detail that you were referring to when you said you would receive detailed instructions from the Main Staff of exactly what was allowed into the enclaves, into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, these permissions, I don't know of any other form, so practically in each one of them, it was written in this way what could enter, total, identification, number, name, quantities, vehicle, persons who were entering, everything. That was the usual form of the permits that I would receive and that I would see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05526 receives number P1507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Nicholls, your last question, could there be any doubt as that this reflects a level of detail? I mean, if you read it, you know it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, but he had -- Your Honours, the reason I did that, he answered a question earlier describing that things were spelled out in detail and I was trying to show this as a typical example confirm that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, having this document in evidence, can see that it's the level of detail apart from what we have -- I think we have similar documents in the past but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There could be possibly no doubt about that, you could even agree on it, that this reflects a level of detail. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm just checking, Your Honours. I may skip a couple documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what they are but if you think it's wise to do it, then do it as you -- or if documents, of course, if you don't need to go through them with the witness, then of course there is still a possibility to bar table them at any future point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on a little bit. Could I have 65 ter 04215, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, this is now in July 1995, 4 July 1995. It's headed "Military Secret, Strictly Confidential, Analysis of combat readiness in the first half of 1995," to the Drina Corps from your brigade, the Bratunac Brigade. And just, if you can with a "yes" or "no," you're familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please go to page 17 of the English, which should be page 31 in the Serbian original?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this report to the Drina Corps, from your brigade, the six-month report on the combat readiness, states: "During 1995, international organisations and their representatives have passed through and stayed temporarily in the brigade's area of responsibility. Their stay and activities in the area of responsibility were monitored and every significant event was promptly reported to the superior organs of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff." Then it says: "In the brigade's area of responsibility, a check-point was established for the control of all international organisations entering and leaving the enclaves of Srebrenica. This check-point functions in accordance with the orders of the Main Staff and instructions and orders of the brigade commander." This is in the intelligence and security section of this report. Could you just tell us if what is written there is accurate based on the situation in that period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I wrote this, and it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04215 receives number P1508, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1508 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what I want to ask you about now is having discussed the way the convoy system worked, and your role in it, checking it at the Yellow Bridge, speaking now about DutchBat and UNPROFOR, what was the effect of the orders passed on by the Main Staff about how much material should be allowed in to resupply DutchBat? In other words, I'm asking you, as head of intel and security and liaison to DutchBat, whether, during this period, let's focus in April, May, June, 1995, if enough material was being allowed in to DutchBat to allow them to carry out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I know for certain is the following: In April, May and June, and until operations began, is the period, that is to say, the three months, where certain restrictions were imposed with regard to DutchBat, but also all of the others who depended on the convoys and who were in Srebrenica. I will focus on DutchBat. Given the fact that I was in permanent contact with them, I can address their requests and I can discuss my analyses that I did concerning DutchBat. I can confirm that there were different restrictions on lubricants, fuels, and on timely rotation of forces in the enclave of Srebrenica that were foreseen to be rotated. They did it from time to time, sending some on leave and bringing in others. I can certainly tell you that it all had a negative impact on the combat readiness and on the implementation of the designated tasks they should have been carrying out in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the impact? If I can just help you, I'll refer to as an example something you testified to in the Tolimir case at T12325. You said that according to your estimates, not even 10 per cent of the fuel required by DutchBat would be allowed in at this time. So what was the effect, you said there was an effect, what was it, of these restrictions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I believe I've answered the question, but I will repeat. If I said there were negative consequences for their combat readiness, the readiness of the protection force's battalion, it entails that they lacked fuel and lubricants to carry out their designated tasks. This entailed the engagement of APCs and everything else that required fuel in order to function -- for the unit to function normally. It includes the hospital, the health clinic, their own premises, generators, APCs, trucks, and everything else. I speak on the basis of my own analyses and on the basis of their objections they forwarded to me and their requests. They asked me to convey to my superior commands that their requests and quantities should be respected. Otherwise, they would be in no position to carry out their designated tasks. As far as I know, although I was not in the enclave, it was all based on their requests sent to me, and it was on the basis of the quantities that eventually entered the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you, Mr. Nicholls referred to your testimony in the Tolimir case, where your estimate was that not even 10 per cent of the fuel required would be allowed in. Is that still your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still claim that the quantities provided were the bare minimum. As an intelligence person, I can discuss assessments based on the elements I had. So it would be in the range of 10 to 15 per cent. I stand by it. That was far from sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, just ten minutes before the break, sir, so I want to ask you now a similar question but regarding the restrictions on humanitarian aid. Based on your knowledge as the intelligence and security officer of the brigade, what was the effect on the Muslim population of the Srebrenica enclave during this period of the amount of supplies allowed in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I assessed the situation in Srebrenica. I received information from the organisations that -- who dealt with civilians and humanitarian assistance. Given the fact that I know that during that period there were constant requests to increase the limited quantities irrespective of the permissions in place, there were, and I need to mention it, oral orders and requests made to me that I be present to control it all. I know precisely that always, on our side, the requests were that some of the quantities envisaged for Srebrenica be provided to the Serb side because the Serb side believed the distribution to be unfair. So there were constant problems in that regard. What was conveyed to me from the ICRC and the UNHCR was that the situation in Srebrenica was terrible, in all respects, health, that there were sick people, that there were many contagious diseases, lice, and that they lacked hygiene items, and that they had insufficient quantities of food. The quantities allowed in were not enough for the people to survive there in rather normal conditions. Based on their reports and statements, the situation was terrible. That was the kind of information I received directly from the people who were in charge of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if you would be interested in taking the break now because I'm now going to go into a completely new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I ask one question. You said those were the reports you received. Did you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of those reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a single reason to do so. My relationship with the people I was in contact with was an honest one and it seems to me that we never tried to cross each other when we discussed either misunderstandings or problems. We were frank, no matter how painful the misunderstandings were or unpleasant for either myself or them. I am 100 per cent convinced that we had a fair relationship, providing accurate information. I have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No only providing accurate information but also receiving accurate information from your counterpart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, always, according to my reports, which I sent, I think the reports were absolutely correct. Of course, to the extent possible to be viewed by them, because the territory was a large one and the issue complex. However, I do believe that, to a large percentage, the reports were accurate, true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will take a break, but could first the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, longer than usual. We will resume at five minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be -- could the accused be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, moving on now, I'm going to move up to the events in July, just before, during and after the fall or liberation of Srebrenica, and what you saw and know happened there. So that's where I'm going. Now, the days leading up, immediately preceding 11 July, do you remember seeing any Drina Corps or Main Staff officers in Bratunac who had come, just prior to the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a number of officers from the Drina Corps command. I also saw a number of officers who arrived from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if you could name them, please. First, from the Main Staff, and then Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From the Main Staff, I saw commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic. I saw Colonel Jankovic, who is also from the Main Staff and their intelligence administration. From the Drina Corps, I saw many officers, including General Krstic, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric, all of the officers who were participating in the activities at the time, starting with Vinko Pandurevic and from the other brigades. They are members of the Drina Corps but they were not from the Main Staff. I saw all of those men in the course of those few days in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talk about Colonel Jankovic from the Main Staff, is that Radoslav Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had Radoslav Jankovic in mind from the intelligence administration of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately what day it was that you first encountered Colonel Jankovic from the Main Staff in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am doubtful as regards that. In any case, what I can recall is that it was on the 8th or the 9th of July. I'm inclined to say that it was the 9th rather than the 8th, although I cannot guarantee that I'm correct. In any case, it was within that period that I saw him at my brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just to be clear, Mirko Jankovic was captain -- or was, sorry, commander of the military police in the Bratunac Brigade. So there were two Jankovics in Bratunac at this time, so we need to be careful. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you just -- can you briefly tell me what you did with Colonel Jankovic from the Main Staff intelligence administration once he arrived, since you were the intelligence officer in Bratunac. If you worked with him, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did, after his arrival in the brigade. Before that, I don't know if he had seen my commander. In any case, he arrived in my office and told me that he came to the Bratunac Brigade, to my sector, on orders of the Main Staff in order to assist me. That is to say that as of the day of his arrival he was to undertake all obligations regarding contact with members of DutchBat and other international organisations in Srebrenica. He also said that as of that moment on, all activities that had to do with intelligence and security, including the drafting of reports to our superior commands, would be done jointly, that is to say, together in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. So just to be very clear, he shared your office while he was working there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As of that date, when he came to my office, until the very end of the operation, when he went back to the Main Staff, he spent time with me and worked in my office. We were sitting in the same office, working together, pertaining to our department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I'm sorry to ask but when approximately will be the next break, just for my planning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next break will be at, let me see, at 12.55, five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Turning now to 11 July 1995, there is evidence in this case already, I believe, about the movement of the population, a large body of people moving from Srebrenica towards Potocari. Can you tell me -- tell the Trial Chamber if you heard about that population movement and when you learned about people going from Srebrenica to the DutchBat base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to be precise on this topic. I had information that people were moving away from the direction of attack of the Serb forces, and that civilians were on the move towards Srebrenica. As for any en masse movement from the area of Srebrenica to the area of Potocari, I received such information and I could see that on the 11th of July, sometime in the afternoon for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And at some point, did you receive information about military-age men or able-bodied men, however you would like to describe them, being present at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of those few critical days, I kept receiving information from the units of my brigade and the infantry battalions. A piece of information on the 11th was, and it was sometime in the afternoon, it arrived from the command of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, that they had observed a large group of civilians moving towards Potocari and the base. As part of that report, they included their assessment, and it was my assessment as well, that in a group that size, there would be also able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At some point did you make an assessment that there were 1500 to 2.000 military-aged able-bodied men at Potocari amongst the crowd?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the assessment of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, that is to say, my subordinates in the battalion command. It was also my assessment based on my previous counter-intelligence assessment on the size and force of the enemy. It was my assessment that in case of an attack or the fall of the enclave of Srebrenica, there would be a number of able-bodied men amongst the population. For the sake of the Chamber I would like to explain what I understood as able-bodied men. The fact that someone is able-bodied does not mean that he was engaged in the military sense. I knew precisely that in Srebrenica the number of able-bodied men was greater than the number of those who were actively involved in the units of the Srebrenica Brigade, that is to say, the Muslim brigade. That was the assessment of the intelligence organ concerning the situation which ensued after the fall of the enclave. So we relied on that figure, that is to say, between 1.000 and 1,500 people, as the number of people who could -- who were able-bodied and who could end up amongst the population in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And I think if I understand your explanation, what you're saying is that not all of those men would be members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: According to my assessments, that is to say, before the fall of the enclave, as well as in the course of those few critical days, it was my assessment that some of the able-bodied men under the then law, well, that would include the category up to 60 or 65 years of age. However, they are still able-bodied and they were duty-bound to join the reserve force if called upon to do so. However, according to my assessment, some of those men were not assigned to the different units of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on a bit now and start talking about the Hotel Fontana meetings in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that, Mr. Nicholls, I have a question on what the witness said a little earlier. Somewhere you said, sir, that you received information and you saw that large groups of people were moving from Srebrenica to Potocari. Just wanted to ask where were you when you did see them, that large group. I'm trying to find out where I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe it's page 40, line 2, Your Honour, or -- line 6 to 11, excuse me, on page 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. At line 10, "I received such information and I could see that on the 11th of July, sometime in the afternoon for the first time." I just wanted to find out where were you at the time when you did see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 11th of July, in the afternoon, several times, not once, I was in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Infantry Battalion in the Kokarde sector and my brigade had an observation post that sector. And several times that day, when the operations started, when the attack on Srebrenica started, on that day, on the 11th, I went to the sector of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, the village and the observation point were called Borici, that's where the observation point was, and from those positions you could clearly see the entire area that was in front of the positions of the 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac 1st Brigade which was in immediate contact with the Potocari sector, and that sector where the civilians were arriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell us, if you heard about -- how you heard about the first Hotel Fontana meeting, how it came up that you learned there was going to be a meeting at the Hotel Fontana, and then after you tell me that, I'll ask you what you did.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The information that a meeting would be held at the Fontana Hotel came to me from Radoslav Jankovic, Colonel. I heard it from him. He told me that members of the DutchBat soldiers and non-commissioned officers or officers, I don't remember their ranks anymore, surrendered and that they were in the Fontana Hotel and they asked for a meeting to be held with General Mladic, and that the attendants at the meeting would include General Ratko Mladic and the head of the DutchBat, Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And what did you do? What was your duty regarding this meeting, talking about the first meeting held on the 11th of July at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic from the Main Staff told me that it was my duty or that we should prepare the place where the meeting was supposed to be held. My task and the task of the military police, the commander of the military police and the police, was to prepare the Fontana Hotel physically for that first and then subsequently the second meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I won't go through all the details of the meeting, but can you tell us where you were during the meeting, whether -- we can see that you're not on the video of that meeting but where were you, what were you doing, during that first meeting at around 8 p.m. on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After we provided security at the Fontana Hotel, after we secured it physically, outside the exit and a part of the reception area using military police, together with Colonel Jankovic and the interpreter Petar, we went inside the hotel to wait for General Mladic. That's where we waited for him. The meeting was held in a small conference room at the hotel. I was to the -- well, to the left, there is a stage where the musicians are supposed to be, so as you look from the entrance to the left that is where I was standing. General Mladic and Karremans went to this small conference room, which has a sliding door, and that is where they went and that was where the first meeting and their first contact took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just a last question on this. Could you observe the meeting from where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could see the participants of the meeting and I could hear what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have basically the same questions for the second meeting, the one that was held later that night with the man this time from the civilians in Potocari. If you could just tell us very briefly what you did in relation to that meeting? Did you secure the area the same way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Exactly the same. My role and the role of the military police regarding the meeting was exactly the same as the first time. So more or less we knew the time, when they were supposed to come to the meeting held at the order of General Ratko Mladic. My task again was to provide the conditions and security for the Hotel Fontana and the area around it, as well as the route the DutchBat took, because -- and possibly members of the Muslim side. At the time I did not know if they would be there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And same thing: Did you observe this meeting without participating in it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Throughout the meeting, the second meeting, I was present in the same area of the Hotel Fontana. I could see who was taking part. I could hear what they were talking about, and at the end of the meeting, pursuant to General Mladic's order, I escorted the participants to Potocari once the meeting was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time of the night-time meetings, had the information -- well, the information would have reached Colonel Jankovic and the Main Staff about the intelligence assessment of the number of men, able-bodied men, if we call them that, in Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All the information, everything that I wrote during those few days, was something that Colonel Jankovic knew because he was sitting in my office. So officially I was in the office, together with Colonel Jankovic, and I wrote intelligence reports to the command of the Drina Corps, and I think this was also sent to the Main Staff, and all the information that we both had at our disposal we knew before we informed the corps command and the Main Staff about them. This information was sent out in written form and we would also send out questions about what it was that we needed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But then just specifically to this information about the 1500 or so men in Potocari, that information was available to the Main Staff by the time of the Potocari meetings? Fontana meetings, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
