utterances.text: In a professional way, in written form, it was addressed to the superior commands, so I can just say that we sent out the information. I assume - I can only assume - that all the key pieces of information arrived at the intended destination along that command line. I cannot comment more on what happened to what we wrote. All I know is that we did write it and send it to the intended recipients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But just last point, I'm just trying to be clear: That was before the last Hotel Fontana meeting that you had sent that information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if you're talk about the last Fontana meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, last Fontana meeting on 11 July, I should clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That late evening meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is how you understood the question as well, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood the question that this was before the last meeting on the 11th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say "we" provided this information and you wrote it up the chain, that is you and Colonel Jankovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the two of us. To be perfectly clear, no document, once he arrived, was sent to the Drina Corps command with either my signature or his signature or just from me or from him. During those days, we were a team that wrote all the reports together. There were no separate reports, one written by me, one written by him. What this means was when it was needed, we would sit at the desk, we would write the information together, or a question, and then we would send it. There were no separate, distinct opinions or information or anything. We would draft it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to move through the chronology of the next couple days. After the second Hotel Fontana meeting on 11 July, what did you do that night? Did you go anywhere and do anything else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After the second meeting, the evening meeting, late-night meeting, after an order by the commander, Mr. Ratko Mladic, I escorted the participants of the second meeting to Potocari. After that, I did not return to the Fontana because there was no need to do that. After that, I went to the command of my own -- the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's move on to 12 July, about what you remember from that morning. Do you recall a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade on the morning of 12 July, including General Mladic and others?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember those meetings. I remember the meeting on the 12th, in the morning, but there were many such meetings. But of course I remember that day. I do need to say that on the 12th of July, from 7 a.m., I was on duty at the Bratunac Brigade command. I was the duty operations officer in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 15141, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I'm about to show you, Mr. Nikolic - and I hope it's clear on your screen - is a report of 12 July 1995. It's a MUP report signed by the chief of the CJB in Zvornik, Dragomir Vasic. I see it's dated 12 July. And the part I'm focusing on is paragraph 2, a meeting with General Mladic and General Krstic was held at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at -- and we have 0800 hours at which tasks were assigned to all those involved. The question is: Do you remember Mr. Vasic being at the brigade or being at this meeting in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did have that noted down in the operations logbook, which I kept meticulously, but I remember that on the 12th, a meeting like this was held in the morning. It's true that I don't know what was discussed at the meeting, but I know that the meeting was attended by those who are referred to here, senior officers from the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that quite a few portions are translated as "illegible." Looking at the original, I wonder what is illegible there. For example, the second it says "illegible of the minister in Pale." Now, I read in the original, "kabinet ministra [phoen] Pale." So same for the "illegible of the police forces in Bijeljina," I see "SSTAB," so I wonder what explains the illegibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have an answer, Your Honour, other than perhaps Ms. Stewart's advised me that it may have -- the translation amy have been from an earlier version that was not good quality, so we could send this for a revision. But it's the same document, but I see you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether it's the same document. If it was another one which was badly legible, I don't know if it's the same, but you apparently are certain of that. The first, for example, says "MUP Republika Srpska." That is, there is no way that it would be illegible. So therefore we will MFI the document, if you would come up with a full translation. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting although this is not my witness. We have to actually object to this document. Obviously there is something in the text, and we saw that previously, that is not in the original. Somebody took the right to explain what some terms mean. So here, in the translation, we have "Turks, derogatory for Muslims." That's not in the document, and we will not accept documents that translate or explain to us what something means. So this is not translation. And we ask the Prosecution to replace this document, if they want to MFI it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it that you want a translation and nothing else, apart from -- are there other matters? Because to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not from my part at this moment. I just wanted to point out this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just "Turks derogatory" -- and I'm also looking one second to -- if you have one second for me. Further down in the text, under paragraph 7, there seems to be something illegible as well. Even there I also have -- so it's not only in the upper part but -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just to say not to MFI it, it's exactly because of our concerns about the accuracy of the translation, whether it's about illegibility or whether it's comments, that we will MFI it. Then it's not in evidence and we will not admit it until we have a full translation and then a translation only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just briefly, Ms. Stewart's informed me she has found another translation which is a -- of the same ERN as the B/C/S original. It does not have the "illegibles" and is a complete translation, so if we can upload that, that may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it also not have the comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can't see it now if it has the comments, Your Honours, but I would just say that that is common in lots of translations in this Tribunal and it's very clear that they are not in the original. So I don't really see a problem with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at the same time, a further explanation of the word "Turks" might not be needed, and let me just -- the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber, of course, observed that on many occasion this kind of interpretation or, you say, comments or explanation is found often and of course often you have not objected to it. So it's not entirely clear to the Chamber why here you do, but technically you're right, it's not translation but comment. At the same time, comment which I think most of us in this courtroom have seen many, many times, especially in relation to this word. But technically you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it's clear that it was added, but we leave it to that. The document will be marked for identification until a new translation without comments is uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we would inquire who added this, whether that was done by CLSS or by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of course it's CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll ask from the CLSS to retranslate and extract these additions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But -- but -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't think CLSS is allowed to tell us what some terms mean. It's not their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if we need a discussion on that, we will have to do it fundamentally because often you have also relied on documents where, for example, acronyms are explained further, so this is not uncommon. But let's not use this document at this moment, but then if you want to make submissions on that matter, of course you're free to do so and then we may have a more fundamental discussion on it. I would say let's try to focus on what really is in dispute, and that Turks -- let's say the following: The evidence shows here and there that "Turks" is a derogatory term for Muslims. That may be clear to everyone in this courtroom. But let's not have it now. New translation. It's MFI'd under what number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is 15141 has been MFI'd under number P1509, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification, therefore. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I take it then we have permission to upload and replace the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the replacement is upon approval by the Chamber, done by the Registrar, and you may upload it. That's the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, without going back to this document in much detail, it refers to that a meeting will be held at 10.00 a.m. with representatives of UNPROFOR and the Muslim representative of Srebrenica, et cetera. Could you tell us how and when you learned of the Hotel Fontana meeting held on the morning of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the last evening -- meeting of that evening of the -- on the 11th of July, General Mladic and Mr. Karremans agreed. And of course at this second night meeting there was a representative of the Muslim civilians, Mr. Mandzic, so it was agreed that the next meeting should be held the following day, on the 12th of July, at the same place in the Hotel Fontana, starting at 10.00, and then the following day, my assignment, the assignment of the military police and everything that happened for the previous two meetings was provided for -- again. The hotel was emptied and security was provided so that that meeting could be held, and it was, in fact, held on the 12th of July at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before the meeting started, did you meet with any Drina Corps Colonels outside the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I arrived much earlier, at the Fontana, before the meeting was supposed to be held because of all the duties I had regarding security, preparation of the space and the police for the meeting, and then sometime before the meeting, I met Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric in front of the Fontana before the meeting began.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you speak with Colonels Popovic and Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did. I spoke with Popovic. Kosoric was also there. Mr. Popovic told me that that day, all the children, women, would be transferred to the territory, meaning that that was more or less the position, the agreement, that they would be transferred to territory under the control of the Muslim forces, meaning Kladanj or Tuzla, or actually meaning that it would be a destination to which they wanted to go. Then he said that able-bodied men would be separated, and to my question, "Lieutenant Colonel, sir, what will happen then with the men," he said arrogantly, "All balijas should be killed." So that is what he said to my question, "What about the men?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please clarify, witness, who said these words? It's not absolutely clear from the transcript. That "all balijas should be killed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic and I had a conversation. It was a face-to-face conversation, and in response to my question, "Lieutenant Colonel, sir," I was addressing Popovic, "what will happen to the men?" He arrogantly, as was his style, said, "All balijas should be killed." So I am conveying, I'm quoting what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then, what further conversation did you and Vujadin Popovic have about the men who were to be killed, the balijas?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have not received interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll try again. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After Popovic told you that all the balijas would be killed -- would be killed, what conversation followed between you and Mr. Popovic, if any, about the execution of these men?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I need to be precise. That's why I have to say this. Before we discussed the executions, there was another topic we discussed. It was the facilities where the separated able-bodied men from Potocari should be accommodated temporarily or imprisoned. Since I originate from Bratunac and it was the area of responsibility of my brigade and I was familiar with the terrain, I told Mr. Popovic that there were facilities, vacant facilities, in Bratunac which could be easily secured with a small number of forces. Those separated at Potocari could be transported and temporarily held in those facilities in Bratunac. I mentioned the Vuk Karadzic primary school, the hangar, the sports gym, and the buildings within that perimeter, which is about 100 metres. All those buildings were in the centre of town, and yet vacant. It was possible to have them secured with a small number of troops. After that, once we were through that topic -- with that topic, two locations were mentioned, where the people should be executed, the people separated at Potocari and transported to Bratunac. The Sase mine was mentioned and the brick factory. I need to say the following as well. At those two locations, no murders took place and there was no organised execution of Muslims there captured there. No one was ever transported to the Sase and the brick factory locations, not a single execution or murder took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, that was quite a long answer. Let me just make sure this is clear. After Vujadin Popovic said all the balijas would be killed, there was a discussion of execution sites and it was suggested that the brick factory and Sase mine could be used as execution sites. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I'm looking at the clock. We are half a minute away from the time of the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can break now, Your Honours, and I'll carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, let me just ask before we move on to another topic, we discussed -- we were just talking now about the discussion -- and you -- and the locations discussed for executions of prisoners were the Sase mine and the brick factory. Did the brick factory have a name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, everyone referred to it as the brick factory. I don't know of any other name. So the Sase mine and Ciglana, meaning the brick factory. It's its original name, I know of no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ciglana was the word I was trying to make clear. Now, if you remember, please tell us, who was it in that conversation between yourself and Mr. Popovic who first mentioned locations in Bratunac for the executions, Ciglana and the Sase mine? Was it you or Mr. Popovic or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In my testimony thus far, because I cannot quote, and I do not recall exactly who mentioned it first, but I do know that first we discussed the facilities for detaining them and then there was a discussion. I was there, Popovic and Kosoric. I truly do not recall who mentioned it first. In any case, all three of us took part in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just, for your memory, read you back a short question and answer about this topic, this is from your testimony in the Blagojevic case, page 1677. 22nd September 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I don't have this in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Q. Were there any locations discussed for the killing of the Muslim men? "A. Yes, yes, Mr. Prosecutor. The places of execution were discussed and two locations were mentioned. The first to be mentioned was the brickworks, the Ciglana, a state-owned company in Bratunac, and the area of the Sase mine in Sase village. "Q. Who brought up these two locations as possible locations for execution? "A. I mentioned both locations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor has quoted already and has been leading for quite a while now. I believe he could have received an answer in a different way. However, I truly need to intervene now, having in mind that he's putting a transcript to his own witness, trying to jog his memory by engaging -- by basically in cross-examination while the witness has already answered. It is a fact that the transcript is in existence, and in it, the witness said what he said, which is that he mentioned the location. However, the witness has already provided an answer during examination-in-chief here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I do not understand either Mr. Nicholls nor you, Mr. Petrusic. First of all, Mr. Nicholls, I do not understand why you would read an answer which is, I'd say, the same answer as the witness gave, that they were mentioned. You can just ask the witness who came up with those names, so therefore I cannot see the use at this moment, but perhaps I'm missing something. At the same time, Mr. Petrusic, I therefore also do not see what is there leading, if you read a portion of a previous testimony, which gives more or less the same answer as the answer already given by the witness. I mean it may be useless but to say it's leading is not what I understand it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- there may be good reasons for that, but I still wonder whether you could have asked who came up with those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, what I did ask him was who was it in the conversation who first mentioned the locations for the executions Ciglana and Sase. That's at page 56, lines 14 to 16. Part of the answer given by Mr. Nikolic on line 20 at page 56 is: "I truly do not recall who mentioned it first." So as he stated he didn't recall who it was in that conversation who first mentioned these two locations as possible execution sites, I was reading back this answer to try to refresh his memory of who it was who first mentioned them, which is contained in the section I'm reading from 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I have to reread it in order to fully -- let me see. My LiveNote is causing me some problems but I'm there now. Let me see. If you just give me a few seconds to read it. Yes. I missed that. I have to apologise for that. But now let's see what you did put to him as a quote. Yes, you're asking the same question, you're not refreshing his memory at this moment yet. You tried again, and then after that I take it that you would -- I don't know what follows in the transcript so I can't tell you whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can just make a quick proffer, Your Honour. In this portion of the transcript from 2003, the witness was asked who first mentioned these two locations as possible locations for execution, and then he gave an answer which answers the question I was trying to refresh his recollection, and I already read out his answer actually at page 57, line 10. Where he had said that in that prior case that he mentioned both locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, then. I am not -- I must admit -- you said 57, line -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's a quote there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a quote there. Yes. Then that is refreshing the memory of the witness. That is okay. I missed that. I apologise for that. I'm not at my best at this very moment because I had forgotten something else as well. That is to inform the parties that Judge Fluegge is for urgent Tribunal reasons unable to continue to sit but only for this last hour of today, and that Judge Moloto and I have considered whether it would be in the interests of justice to continue to hear this case and we decided it was. That's the reason why there are two Judges. That's not my best performance, Mr. Nicholls, neither the intervention in the last one nor the 15 bis. I'll try to improve my performance. Please proceed, the objection is denied, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, it's been a while since I read out this portion to try to refresh your recollection, but in short, what I read out, in Blagojevic, when you were asked who brought up these two locations as possible locations for execution, you answered: "A. I mentioned both locations," but let me read the complete answer in fairness, "but in view of the way in which they reacted, my conclusion was that they already knew, that is, that they both knew them already, knew about both locations." So having heard that, your testimony from ten years ago, actually, does that help you remember who first mentioned Sase mine and Ciglana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My answer is as follows: We were discussing those places, and I said that in my first testimony in the Blagojevic case, and in all subsequent evidence. I believe that it was irrelevant. All three of us discussed the locations for executions. If I said that it was me ten years ago, which I truly do not recall anymore, and I can't quote myself, but if I did say at the time, ten years ago, that I brought it up, I don't have a problem with acknowledging or accepting that. However, all three of us were discussing the locations. So I see nothing controversial in accepting this as something that I did say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, where this conversation took place, where was it in relation to the Hotel Fontana, the conversation between you, Mr. Popovic and Mr. Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That conversation was in front of the Fontana Hotel, in front of the entrance. It was a conversation, but it was not a meeting. It happened before the meeting, and had this conversation of between five and ten minutes, but I don't recall it very well. The conversation took place before the meeting scheduled for 10.00 on the 12th of July. It was just before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you attend the third Hotel Fontana meeting in the sense of were you present during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you mean whether I was physically present in the Fontana Hotel, I was not present in the area where the meeting took place. Throughout that time, I was in front of the hotel at the reception, and in that area, making sure that the security measures that were undertaken for the meeting were in place. I did see, though, all those who came and entered the hotel to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear, then. What happened after the meeting? What were your next duties? What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Following the meeting, the participants came out, including Colonel Radoslav Jankovic. He told me that the next thing that had to be done, the next task, for all of us, including myself, was to work on evacuation - I called it forcible transfer - of the population to Muslim-held territory. Of course, the people from Potocari. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then where did you go? Did you go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: For a while, I stayed in front of the Fontana Hotel. Perhaps some half an hour later, I saw two or three DutchBat officers arrive. I talked to them in front of the Fontana, and Petar Uscumlic and Kosoric were present as well. They were interested in buses. In front of the Fontana Hotel, there was Colonel Acamovic at the time. I think Colonel Krsmanovic was there too. They were from the logistics of the Drina Corps. I told them to discuss it with them to obtain all information regarding transport and the arrival of buses. After that, I went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I seek on two points of clarification, Mr. Nicholls, the first is was about who mentioned the sites, the suggested sites of execution first. Mr. Petrusic, I'm especially addressing you. The witness more or less said, If I said this in one of the previous cases, then he says, I do not challenge that, I accept that. Now, of course we haven't seen the transcript. Is there any challenge on the Defence side on the accuracy of the quote given by Mr. Nicholls? Because that is relevant for the appreciation of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will not question the quote from page 1677 from 2003 in the Blagojevic case. We do not dispute that it is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear. Then I have another question for you, Witness. You said that on from a certain moment, that the work to be done was evacuation, and you said, "I called it forcible transfer of the population." Which I understand to mean that they were not free to choose but that they had to leave. Is that what you intended when you said, "I called it forcible transfer"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an explanation for what I said and it is as follows: If we look at it from the legal point of view, officially, and if we take into account what kind of choice was presented to them, then in legal and formal terms they could choose whether to stay or leave. However, if we view it from a different angle, from the human angle, I would say, in my view, I know the people. I know the mentality of the people. None of the people in Potocari would voluntarily leave their house and property and everything they had in their lives and say, "Well, now I will voluntarily go to Kladanj to be a refugee, leaving behind everything I have acquired in my lifetime." From that point of view, as for the reason why they were leaving, why they were leaving their house, property and everything they owned, the reason was simply because after the operation, after everything that took place, it was their assessment that remaining there would be unsafe. They believed it wouldn't be safe to go on living there in the circumstances created after the fall of Srebrenica. That is why I believe, I think, that none of those people, hosts, left Potocari and Srebrenica because they liked to go. They left because they were forced to. The issue was that of safety and existence, and further action, because that was the very end of the operation, the end of the war in that area. That is why I called it forcible transfer of civilians. Of course, it is my opinion. None of the things I mentioned, as security and safety aspects, could be guaranteed to them by anyone. You could tell them, yes, we will guarantee this or that, and then you choose, but in practice, I claim that could not be provided, especially in the moments of the enclave's fall, when it was taken. That is why, and I could explain it in different ways, but this is the basic thing why I consider it to be a forcible transfer of the population from their hearths, from the -- to another part of the country which is where they felt safer and which was at the time controlled by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. You may proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to ask you, again, just going through the chronology, after this third Hotel Fontana meeting, you talked about staying there for about half an hour. Where did you go next, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After that, I went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you just tell us, as best as you can, when -- well, first of all, approximately what time did you get to Potocari, approximate, on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I recall is, I think twice or thrice I was in Potocari before the transport began but I think it was sometime after 12.00, that was the first time I went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us first which -- personnel from which units of the VRS or MUP did you see present in Potocari when you went there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you one thing, which I believe is important, regarding the units. Before I went to Potocari, and before Colonel Jankovic told me that assistance had to be provided during the evacuation or the forcible transfer, I asked him what kind of units were engaged and what needed to be done. He literally told me that there are no problems in that area, that the units in charge of the evacuation from Potocari had already been assigned their tasks and that some of those units with their commanders were already in Potocari. I can enumerate more or less the units engaged up there. I'll start with my brigade. Part of the Bratunac Brigade military police was engaged. Then there was a unit which carried out an attack from the area of Pribicevac. It arrived around that time in the area of Potocari. Next, parts of my 2nd Infantry Battalion were engaged. The Wolves from the Drina were there. They were members of the Zvornik Brigade. There were different kinds of police units. For example, members of the public security station from Bratunac, then members of the special brigade of the MUP of Republika Srpska. There was a company, a police company, of the PJP. And there was a unit, I don't know what its name was, though, but they all had police dogs with them. I think, or actually I'm sure, that there were parts of the police force from the 65th Protection Regiment from Nova Kasaba, and I think there were individuals or a group from the 10th Sabotage Detachment, which is a unit of the Main Staff of the VRS. I don't think I have omitted anyone. Sorry, there were also parts of the military police from the MP Battalion of the Drina Corps. I don't think I forgot anyone. Those were the forces which at that moment were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that detailed answer. Now, in the same vein, could you tell me who you observed in Potocari -- are you okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Am I okay? Yes, I am. I was listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which officers, if any, did you see from the Main Staff in Potocari when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will be precise. It was perhaps not on the first occasion, but I did tell you I was in Potocari a few times. And what I believe is important is to say that I was there at the moment when evacuation began. Or the forcible transfer. On that occasion, I saw General Ratko Mladic in Potocari and I saw quite a number of officers from the brigades which were engaged in the attack. I saw Ljubisa Borovcanin, who was deputy commander of the special brigade, as well as different security organs, and officers, members of the State Security Service and so on and so forth. I saw many people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask some names then. Did you see Colonel Jankovic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was there countless times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you see anybody from Drina Corps intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There was Popovic and Kosoric, and from the Drina Corps there was Acamovic, Krsmanovic, so the first two -- the two are from the intelligence department and the other two were assistant commander for the logistics and the head of the traffic service. I saw them in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us what you saw happening to the civilian population in Potocari when you were there, regarding the men, the women and the children, how they were treated and what happened to them, if you could describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of evacuation, in the area between where the civilians were on one side and the area where they were supposed to go, where the buses had arrived, there was a ribbon placed there. It was a kind of delineation mark where the civilians were. Order was kept by members of DutchBat, the police and the forces which happened to be there at the time. The first convoy, the first getting on board, occurred without any separation. Men were not separated from women and children. They all simply went as they were directed. From one side, from the direction of Bratunac, on the right-hand side, there was a passage, a free passage, which could be used by the people going to the buses to get on. At first, it resembled a normal process of having them transported. At some point, however, there was general commotion and people shoving and everything was stopped. After that, separations occurred, a selection. What I do know is that the reason why it was ordered at first was that the women and children should apparently be -- have priority and then the men would be let through later. And that's when the selection, the separation of men from women and children, took place. The men were taken on one side and the children and women to the buses. Then the men who were separated were escorted by the police or soldiers who were there to the nearby buildings, houses, where they were placed. What I could see, and it was also the first signal which indicated to me that something was wrong, was the way the people separating them were treating them like. They first of all took all of their personal belongings, creating an enormous pile of plastic bags and everything they carried, and then they took them there. They insulted them, maltreated them, hit them, spat on them. They said things to them. That's what I could see in that area while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you say these persons who were separated and had their belongings taken away and were hit and spat, is that referring to Muslim men, what happened to the men who were separated and then taken to houses?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 19562, please. Now, this is a document dated 12 July. It's got 1730 hours at the top on the left, very urgent, and it says "Drina Corps IKM Bratunac." If we go to page 2 of the English, please, all right, there we can see paragraph 3, and to save time I won't read the whole paragraph out. It talks about the numbers of women and children and the elderly and the sick, how many people have been evacuated so far. But the last sentence says: "We are separating men from 17 to 60 years of age and we are not transporting them." Sorry, that's the penultimate sentence. Then: "We have about 70 of them so far, and the security organs and the DB," state security, CLSS has added, "are working with them." And it's from Lieutenant Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How does that last couple sentences in Popovic's report, how does that fit with what you saw and what you told us? Is what he's saying here accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right. You directed me to this third paragraph and what it says here, mostly, was my estimate as well, and that of Colonel Jankovic, regarding the number of these people, 30 to 35, to 40.000 people. These are the estimates. And I agree this is what our estimate was as well. As for what it says in the last sentence, these are men, those who happened to be among the civilians in Potocari, and at this point of time he's reporting about how many of them were captured and placed in the building or facility that I mentioned a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when he says about 70 of them so far, does that seem right based on your experience or does it seem high or low or about right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the number is based on here, but I cannot debate what he's saying here. What I know is what I wrote in my report, and what my estimate was, and that is that after that first day, between 350 and 400 men were separated and then they were transferred to these facilities. This is after the first day. The first day of the transport was on 12 July. After the second day, there was a slightly smaller number than the first day, but it is my estimate and that of Colonel Jankovic, based on what we saw and knew, is that approximately, during those two days, about 600 to 650 to 700 men were separated. These were all estimates. We didn't count them, take their names, but these are estimates based on what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19562 receives number P1510, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1510 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said that on the -- I don't have it in front of me, but words to the effect, just a minute ago, that on the first convoy out there was no separation and that men were able to get on it, that convoy. Do you recall whether that convoy, with men on it, was filmed or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I saw then, and then later, over the public information media, is that the first convoy, the first departure, and the conversation and interviews with certain officers in Potocari was later broadcast by the press service of the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And you've testified about this before, but based on being there, being an intel and security officer, what was the purpose of filming those men getting on the first convoy?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That act in itself, right from the start, was something that nobody knew where that would go, what would happen. What I know is that after that convoy, there were no more men in the buses, and I know that later the filming, the photographing, was used as something indicating that nothing unusual or bad happened, but that everything proceeded properly. So then and now, my conclusion is that that filming or photographing was misused and used for propaganda purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when these men, Muslim men, were separated in Potocari and put in these houses, captured, as you said a minute ago, did you see any screening process? Was there any screening, checking of these men to see if they were war criminals? Did any of the men leave the house and then be allowed to get on convoys? In other words, was there any screening whatsoever of the men you saw being separated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. What I know, as an intelligence security organ, is that in such operation, military triage is a militarily legitimate act. On the basis of indicia and prior information, you would perform regular military triage. This is not something that was done. Perhaps somebody else knows but I don't know of any cases that somebody was questioned, listed and then checked or vetted and then released. I know two individual cases. I know of a Muslim deputy who was handed over to the state security and I know of one wounded person taken over by the State Security Service. Those are the two cases that I know of. In Potocari, there was no military triage and there were none who were returned to join their family after their -- they were questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have, very quickly, 65 ter 04067. While it's coming up, this is a document dated 13 July 1995. It's an RDB document, state security. It's to the deputy of -- Minister of the Interior personally to the head of the RS MUP Bijeljina. We don't need to go to the second page but there it shows that it's signed by RDB head Dragan Kijac or, rather, type-signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we look at the first paragraph, Mr. Nikolic, it talks about captures of Muslim soldiers, which I'm not going to get into now, but at the bottom of that first paragraph, it states that: "The operation is continuing and the movement of the Muslim column," which we will talk about later, "has been confirmed many times in interviews with prisoners." And then a little further on it says: "Igban Mustafic, a former SDA deputy in the former BH Assembly and a great opponent of Naser Oric, was among the prisoners and can, with the necessary preparation, be used well in the media." And the question is: Is that man listed here, Mr. Mustafic, is this the incident you are referring to when you said that a prisoner was taken over by state security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I talked about Ibran Mustafic specifically. Before the war, in the first multi-party elections, he was a deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that Zlatan Celanovic also went. They called that processing, meaning that he questioned Ibran Mustafic regarding the activities there. There is another person, I think that he was wounded, his name was Halilovic, for whom there were indications that he had committed war crimes. He was separated, taken to Zvornik, and processed by the MUP, but I don't know the outcome. I don't know what happened to him. In any event, I know of these two cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04067 receives number P1511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1511 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Can you just round off the 12th of July for us? Where did you go after your final point of time in Potocari? What did you do that night?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony, I already said that I was the duty operations officer on the night of the 12th and 13th of July. A number of times, depending on the need, I went to Potocari and I went back. I spent some of the time in the operations room and a part of the time in Potocari. When that day was over, I went to the operations room or centre and I was on duty that night, which means that I was in the operations room until 3.00 a.m. Before I went to sleep, after I came back to the operations room, I informed my commander about all the activities and I wrote a report about all intelligence information that I had at my disposal that day. I also sent that to the Drina Corps command. After midnight, sometime around 3.00 in the morning, Mirko Jankovic came, who was my deputy, and he relieved me of duty. He stayed in the duty operations room and I went to sleep. And I slept perhaps for two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, is it 2.15 we go to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Then let's continue now just with the chronology, sir. 13 July, if you could tell us, I think you went to Potocari that day again. I don't think my friends mind me leading that way. Can you tell us what happened on the morning of 13 July when you got up and what you did before going to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I've already said, this was already the 13th of July, at 3.00 I went to sleep and I slept. And then, if I remember correctly, at about 7 a.m. I returned to the Bratunac Brigade command. I came to the duty operations room, and I think that I just carried out all the formalities regarding the handover of duty. I think I also wrote in something in the duty operations logbook. These are just regular activities. And then of course I saw my commander, of course, Vidoje Blagojevic. And then after that I was simply told that, on the 13th, the activities started on the 12th in Potocari would continue and that my first assignment would be to go to Potocari and to see what was happening there. Of course, I went to Potocari and saw what was happening in Potocari. The evacuation was already underway, the buses started arriving. I did not walk around, but I got in touch with Dusko Jevic on the 13th and I told him then, if he was in radio contact with units engaged on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, he should convey the information to them that those who were captured in that area should be transferred to the detention facility in Baljkovica [as interpreted], and then I told him to move some 50 or 100 metres away from where he was working to a broader -- a wider area. On the 13th, the evacuation from Potocari continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. Let me just ask you, the transcript says, when you spoke to Dusko Jevic you said that captured prisoners should be transferred to a detention facility in Baljkovica. You testified before they should be transferred to Bratunac. Can you just check that transcript for us if that's the right -- if what we see there is right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, perhaps I made a slip. I never said Baljkovic or Baljkovica. I said that the prisoners should be transferred to the detention facilities in Bratunac. These were the facilities allocated for that purpose on the 12th. I said if they were in contact with the forces engaged in that direction, I said that all those detained should be transferred to the facilities in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We only have five minutes left. If you could just tell the Trial Chamber quickly, what information did you have at the 13th -- on the 13th of July, when you were speaking with Mr. Dusko Jevic about the movement of the Muslim column through the forest?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Already on the 12th, in the afternoon, and to a good part on the 13th, we, or, rather, I had information about the movement of an armed column of Muslims from two sectors, the sector of Jaglici towards Konjevic Polje, Cerska and farther, and from the Susnjari sector also towards Konjevic Polje and farther. Cerska and farther. Also, on the 13th already we had information from the neighbouring unit, from the Milici Brigade, that also in the area of responsibility of their brigade there were already captured Muslims or those who had surrendered. And also on the 13th already, on the mentioned roads, I had information that there was sporadic fighting already, there was shooting, there were woundings, and one policeman died in the Sandici sector. And I had information that in that area, along that axis, there were prisoners and there were already groups surrendering to the Serbian side. This is the most general type of information that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we talked about -- you explained how men were separated in Potocari and then brought to Bratunac. Muslim men who were captured or surrendered along this Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road, were they treated the same or any differently from the men who had been separated in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I saw, and I did see captured individuals on that road, I saw individuals, groups, and large groups that were captured on that sector, and their status of prisoners was the same as in Potocari. They were searched, their items were put to the side, their valuables were confiscated. And of course, after that, they were detained in the temporary facilities in Konjevic Polje where the 5th Engineering Battalion of the Drina Corps was billeted, and then in the school. And then after that, in the same way as these others, they were transported in buses to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This would be a good time for me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Moloto has one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, at page 74, lines 15 to 17, you said: "I stayed if --" and I suspect you wanted to say "I said." "I stayed if they were in contact with the forces engaged in that direction, I said all those detained should be transferred to the facilities in Bratunac." Just two questions. Do you know whether they were indeed transferred to the facilities in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to which facilities in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the facilities of the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, the sports hall of the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, the hangar, and one old school of the Djuro Pucar Stari high school centre, until they were full. After that, those who were transferred were held in buses and trucks that they had been brought in and they were guarded by the police forces, military, and, in the end, by civilians who were engaged to do this later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one transcript correction I've been reminded of. At page 6, line 7, this is a minor point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 6, line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it says that Mr. Nikolic pleaded guilty in 1993, it should be 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that may be obvious and is hereby corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Nikolic, we will adjourn for the day. Your testimony will not be resumed tomorrow but only at the beginning of next week. Meanwhile, you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or testimony still to be given. And I instruct you to refrain from doing that. Not to speak, not to communicate, any other way. If that is clear to you, the witness can be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I am aware of all my obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I see that you're on your feet. If you would like to raise the matter I'll address now, then let's see what happens. I do understand and I've seen that a new translation has been uploaded for P1509 MFI'd. That new translation, Mr. Lukic, no illegible portions are found there anymore, but the explanation of Turks as derogatory for Bosnian Muslims remains. Now, the Chamber has considered your objection against that to be admitted and rejects that, unless you would want to say anything further on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will raise this issue in one general motion where we will ask for all those interpretations to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me say the following. I give you the reasons why the Chamber rejects your objection at this moment. A literal translation often does not bring the real --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Lukic. I was about to give the reasons. A literal translation of a word often does not give the real meaning of that word in the context. For example, here, if you would translate it by Turkish or Turks, then the ordinary understanding of that word is a person of Turkish nationality or origin, whereas in this context, it has a different meaning. It is common that where a literal translation is not -- does not -- is not an accurate translation, then CLSS will usually provide a very short explanation for the meaning of that word in the given context. That is what happens here. The appropriate way of dealing with it would be to challenge the explanation. So if you say "Turks" is not in this context a derogatory word for Bosnian Muslims, then we could discuss that, but it is on this basis that a literal translation would not do and this explanation is, as the Chamber is aware of, is quite commonly used, that we admit into evidence P1509. But first, Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the English translation of this document by the newly uploaded translation, doc ID 01776571 ET and P1509 is admitted into evidence. We are looking forward to any further submissions on the general system, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure that we have in previous cases dealt with the same issue in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then see that and we will seriously of course pay attention to it. We adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 31st of May, 2013, in this same courtroom, III, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of May, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
